summaries.example: Imagine two number puzzles. To check whether two numbers share only 1 as a common factor, you can use Euclid’s method and finish with a number of steps that grows fairly slowly as the numbers get longer. To try every possible route through many cities, however, may require checking an enormous number of routes. Complexity theory compares these growth patterns.
summaries.summary: Computational complexity theory studies how difficult problems are for algorithms. It asks how the time and memory needed by the best methods grow when inputs become larger. This is different from asking only whether a problem can be solved eventually. For example, Euclid’s algorithm checks whether two numbers are relatively prime with relatively few steps, while trying every possible tour through many cities can take an enormous number of steps. Complexity theory places problems into classes such as P and NP. P contains problems with polynomial-time methods. NP contains problems for which a proposed yes-answer can be checked in polynomial time, using the theory’s formal model. The famous question P = NP? asks whether quickly checking answers is, in the important general sense, as easy as finding them. The entry also explains that these ideas matter beyond computer programs: they help us think about logical reasoning, mathematical proofs, knowledge, and the limits imposed by limited time and memory.
key_ideas: A problem may be solvable in principle but still be too slow for practical use.
The size of an input matters: a number’s written length can be much shorter than the number itself.
Polynomial-time methods are commonly treated as feasible, while exponential-time methods are commonly treated as difficult.
P is contained in NP, but whether P and NP are actually different is still an open question.
Complexity theory also connects computing with logic, mathematics, proof, and ideas about knowledge.
summaries.why_it_matters: Complexity theory helps explain why some tasks work well on a computer while others become unmanageable as they grow. It gives careful meanings to words such as “easy,” “hard,” and “feasible,” instead of relying only on intuition. Its questions also affect how we think about finding proofs, checking explanations, planning, games, and what people or machines can know or do within limited resources.

important_terms.definition: A question with a yes-or-no answer, such as “Is this number prime?”
A clear set of steps for solving a problem.
The amount of time or memory an algorithm may need as its input becomes larger.
A group of problems that can be solved within a certain kind of time or memory limit.
A class of problems solvable in polynomial time, a growth pattern often used as a standard for practical feasibility.
A class of problems whose yes-answers can be checked quickly when a suitable answer or certificate is supplied.

questions_to_think_about: Why can writing a very large number be easy even when working with it may be hard?
Would a method that checks a proposed answer quickly always be able to find that answer quickly?
Why might two problems that can both be solved eventually have very different practical difficulty?

summaries.example: Consider SAT: given a propositional formula, is there an assignment of true and false values that makes it true? A proposed assignment can be checked in polynomial time, so SAT belongs to NP. Yet the straightforward search may examine exponentially many assignments. SAT is NP-complete, meaning every problem in NP can be transformed into it by a polynomial-time reduction. Therefore, a polynomial-time algorithm for SAT would give polynomial-time algorithms for every NP problem. This does not prove that SAT is outside P; it explains why its status is central to the P versus NP question.
summaries.summary: Computational complexity theory classifies the difficulty of solving decision problems about finite combinatorial objects. Its central concern is not mere effective decidability—whether some procedure eventually halts with the right answer—but resource-bounded decidability. Algorithms are compared by worst-case time and space as functions of encoded input length, with polynomial and exponential growth providing especially important contrasts. The class P contains problems decidable in polynomial time on a conventional deterministic Turing-machine model. NP can be described through nondeterministic polynomial time or, more informally, through the existence of polynomial-size certificates whose correctness can be checked in polynomial time. Deterministic simulation shows that nondeterminism does not enlarge the class of computable problems, although it may create an exponential time gap. Polynomial-time reductions organize the internal structure of classes, and NP-complete problems are the hardest members of NP under these reductions. SAT, traveling-salesperson decision problems, and several graph problems are examples. The conjecture P ≠ NP would formalize the belief that efficiently verifying a solution is not generally as easy as finding one. The entry emphasizes that this remains unproved, while other separations, such as P properly contained in EXP, are known. It also discusses related classes, logical characterizations, proof complexity, quantum and probabilistic computation, and philosophical questions about feasibility, knowledge, and bounded reasoning.
key_ideas: Computability in principle and feasible computability are different notions: a problem can have a halting algorithm while lacking a practically efficient one.
Complexity is assigned to families of finite instances and is measured using resources such as worst-case time, space, and input length.
The Cobham-Edmonds idea treats polynomial-time computation as a mathematical analysis of feasibility, supported by robust simulations across reasonable machine models.
Nondeterminism does not add new computable problems, but it can make polynomial-time verification appear possible even when deterministic simulation may require exponential time.
Reductions explain why apparently different tasks—logic, graphs, scheduling, and routing—can share the same intrinsic difficulty.
Many class separations remain unresolved. In particular, P is known to be properly contained in EXP, but whether P is properly contained in NP is open.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory supplies a framework for distinguishing limits caused by an algorithm from limits caused by the problem itself. It informs the analysis of planning, logical validity, proof search, graph problems, cryptographic tasks, and games. Philosophically, it sharpens questions about feasible computation: mathematical computability allows procedures with astronomically large resource demands, whereas ordinary reasoning and practical technology are resource-bounded. Complexity results therefore bear on what counts as usable knowledge, whether checking can differ fundamentally from discovering, and how formal models should represent limited rational agents.

important_terms.definition: A yes-or-no problem represented as a set of finite encoded inputs; deciding it means accepting exactly the members of that set.
The number of basic computational steps, usually considered in the worst case, as a function of input length.
The amount of working storage used by a computation, measured as a function of input length.
The length of an encoded input, rather than the numerical value it represents; this distinction is crucial for numerical problems.
The class of problems decidable by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time; it is used as a formal standard of feasible decidability.
The class of problems decidable in polynomial time by a nondeterministic Turing machine, equivalently characterized informally by polynomial-size certificates verifiable in polynomial time.
A transformation computable in polynomial time that converts membership in one problem into membership in another.
A problem in a class that belongs to the class and is at least as difficult as every problem in that class under the chosen reductions.

questions_to_think_about: Does polynomial time capture everything that should count as feasible, given that its constants and exponents may be very large?
Why does a polynomial-time reduction show that an efficient method for one problem would help solve another?
What is the philosophical difference between knowing that a proof exists and being able to find or understand one within feasible limits?
If nondeterministic computation can be simulated deterministically, why is NP still believed to be larger than P?

summaries.example: Suppose a school wants to visit several towns and return home while staying under a fuel budget. One approach lists every possible visiting order. With a few towns this works, but each extra town can make the list grow extremely quickly. This is a brute-force method. Complexity theory asks whether a much faster method exists and compares this task with others, such as checking a proposed route or checking a proposed truth assignment for a logic puzzle.
summaries.summary: Computational complexity theory studies how much time and memory different kinds of problems require. It focuses on problems about finite objects—such as numbers, formulas, graphs, routes, and game positions—and measures difficulty by the resources used by the best available algorithms. This adds an important layer to computability theory. Computability asks whether a procedure can eventually give the right answer; complexity asks whether the procedure remains workable as inputs grow. Polynomial-time computation is commonly treated as a mathematical standard for feasibility, while exponential growth is commonly associated with intractability. These standards are expressed through complexity classes. P contains problems solvable in polynomial time by a deterministic machine. NP contains problems whose positive answers can be verified quickly when a suitable certificate is supplied, and it can also be defined using nondeterministic computation. The two classes are known to satisfy P ⊆ NP, but it remains open whether the inclusion is proper. Reductions compare problems: if one problem can be converted efficiently into another, an efficient method for the second would help solve the first. NP-complete problems are both in NP and at least as difficult as every NP problem. SAT, traveling-salesperson decision problems, and several graph problems are examples. The entry also distinguishes computational complexity from related notions such as the compressibility of an individual object and the efficiency of one particular algorithm. Finally, it connects complexity with logic, proofs, mathematical knowledge, bounded rationality, probabilistic computation, and quantum computation.
key_ideas: Complexity theory separates “solvable eventually” from “solvable efficiently enough to matter in practice.”
Input length is important because a compact numeral can represent a very large number.
P is used as a formal model of feasible computation, although the fit with everyday practice has qualifications.
NP problems may have quickly checkable certificates even when no quick method for finding them is known.
NP-complete problems are linked by reductions, so an efficient solution to one would efficiently solve every problem in NP.
The relationship among P, NP, coNP, PSPACE, and other classes contains major unanswered questions.
summaries.why_it_matters: Complexity theory helps us talk carefully about practical difficulty. A problem may be decidable in principle yet unusable for large inputs. This matters in planning, scheduling, logical reasoning, proof checking, games, and other activities involving many possible choices. The theory also raises philosophical questions: Is “feasible” a precise mathematical idea or only an approximation to ordinary practice? Does quick verification imply quick discovery? And should a theory of knowledge take account of the limited time and memory available to people?

important_terms.definition: A problem that asks for a yes-or-no decision about an input.
A step-by-step procedure that solves a problem.
A measure of how computation grows as the input gets larger, especially in time or memory.
The encoded length of an input, used to judge how much work an algorithm requires.
A collection of problems solvable in polynomial time by a standard deterministic machine model.
A collection of problems for which a proposed yes-answer can be verified in polynomial time; it is also defined using nondeterministic machines.
A short object or proposed solution that allows a machine to verify a yes-answer efficiently.
A method for turning instances of one problem into instances of another while preserving yes and no answers, with only polynomial-time work.

questions_to_think_about: Is a problem really easy if its running time is polynomial but its exponent is enormous?
Why might checking a route or assignment be easier than discovering one?
How can reductions reveal a connection between logic puzzles and travel planning?
Should a problem count as feasible when it is fast on average but slow in the worst case?
